passage.title: When More Data Produces Less Knowledge

paragraphs.text: A research team installs thousands of sensors in a building and suddenly has more readings than it can inspect. Temperature, vibration, humidity, occupancy, and energy use appear in a dashboard every few seconds. The charts reveal patterns that a monthly inspection would miss. Yet when a machine fails, the team still cannot say which change caused the failure. The central question is uncomfortable: how can a project accumulate more information while making little progress toward explanation?

Sensors expand what can be observed, but they do not decide what matters. A reading is produced by a device, at a location, at a time, under a particular calibration. If one sensor is moved or replaced, its values may shift even if the environment has not. If many sensors report correlated changes, they may all be responding to one shared condition. A large dataset can therefore contain repeated measurements of the same underlying event rather than many independent clues.

One tempting approach is to search automatically for variables that move together. Suppose vibration rises shortly before a shutdown. This association can help predict that another shutdown is likely, even if vibration is not the cause. A hidden change in load could increase both vibration and failure risk. Or a technician may inspect a machine more often when it sounds unusual, making the recorded maintenance rate rise at the same time. Correlation can guide investigation without settling what produced the pattern.

The distinction between prediction and explanation is practical. An alarm that reliably warns of failure may be valuable, even before engineers know why it works. But a manager deciding whether to reduce machine load needs to know whether load causes the failures or merely accompanies them. If the team changes the wrong variable, the alarm may continue while output falls. The same data can support a useful forecast and remain insufficient for a causal claim.

A causal hypothesis narrows the question. Instead of asking which readings correlate with shutdowns, researchers might ask whether high operating load raises failure risk by increasing heat. That proposal identifies a mechanism and suggests what to measure: load, temperature, cooling behavior, and breakdown timing. It also allows a prediction that could fail. If high load occurs without added heat or failure under specified conditions, the proposed mechanism needs revision.

Testing the idea requires comparisons that separate competing explanations. Engineers can examine similar machines operating at different loads, while accounting for age and maintenance. If safe, a controlled change in load can provide stronger evidence than observing machines that differ in many ways. Yet the intervention itself may alter cooling or operator behavior. A test is informative only when the team records what changed, what stayed comparable, and which outcomes were measured.

Data volume can make this design problem harder. When analysts search thousands of possible relationships, some will appear striking by chance. A pattern discovered after repeated adjustments may not recur in new data. Dividing records into exploration and confirmation sets helps, but it does not repair a poorly chosen measurement or an unrepresentative sample. More computing can find more candidate patterns; it cannot guarantee that those patterns correspond to stable causes.

The team also needs to seek counterexamples. If the hypothesis says heat causes failure, researchers should inspect machines that became hot but did not fail, as well as failures without unusual heat. These cases can reveal conditions the hypothesis omitted, such as different materials or cooling systems. Analysts often focus on observations that fit a favored explanation because they make a coherent story. A deliberate search for cases that should contradict the story is a stronger test.

A counterexample does not always disprove a causal claim. A mechanism may operate only above a threshold or in combination with another condition. However, adding exceptions after every contrary result can make a hypothesis impossible to test. Researchers need to state the relevant conditions in advance when possible. A useful explanation should say not only what pattern it predicts, but also where the prediction should stop applying.

Measurement quality limits conclusions. A temperature sensor near the casing may miss heat in a moving part; a slow sampling rate may miss a brief spike. Missing values may occur when power is unstable, making gaps informative rather than random. Before concluding that temperature was unrelated to failure, the team must know whether its instrument could register the change.

Researchers can combine sensor logs with maintenance notes, operator reports, and part replacements. These sources may disagree in timing or terminology. A technician might describe a sound as “rough,” while the dashboard records vibration. Joining records requires interpretation; a mismatch may reflect different definitions rather than error. The goal is not to replace measurement with anecdote, but to understand each source.

Once the team defines a hypothesis, chooses measurements, and looks for counterexamples, it may conclude that a smaller dataset is more useful than the full stream. A carefully selected comparison can isolate a question better than a dashboard containing every possible variable. The discarded readings are not necessarily worthless; they may help test a different question later. But collecting everything without a plan can increase storage and analytic burden while making attention more diffuse.

There is no universal rule that fewer data produce better science. A sensor network can reveal rare events, spatial differences, and sequences that sparse observation would miss. The relevant issue is whether the data are linked to a question and a credible comparison. If the system measures variables poorly, ignores alternative explanations, or tests its story on the same observations that suggested it, expanding the network may intensify confidence without strengthening evidence.

More measurements can improve knowledge when they make a hypothesis testable, reveal an unexpected counterexample, or distinguish rival explanations. They can also multiply associations without identifying causes. Understanding grows not simply with the number of readings, but with the discipline used to select, compare, and challenge them. The team’s best next step may be another sensor, a controlled test, or a better question; only a clear explanation of the uncertainty can tell which one is needed.

questions.stem: How does the passage distinguish prediction from causal explanation?

choices.text: Vibration could predict shutdown while sharing a hidden cause with failure, leaving its usefulness insufficient to identify effective interventions.
choices.rationale: Association can support forecasting while leaving causation unresolved.

choices.text: A reliable warning identifies a causal factor, although further measurements are needed to estimate how strongly it affects failure.
choices.rationale: Prediction can reflect a hidden shared cause rather than identifying causality.

choices.text: A pattern explains failure when it appears before shutdown, while prediction requires that it recur across several machines.
choices.rationale: Temporal order alone does not establish cause; recurrence is not the defining distinction.

choices.text: Prediction concerns correlated sensor values, while explanation becomes available once maintenance reports describe the same observed pattern.
choices.rationale: Adding another description does not alone distinguish rival causal explanations.

questions.stem: What makes a causal hypothesis more useful than an unrestricted search for correlations?

choices.text: A specific hypothesis selects relevant readings, allowing correlated variables outside the proposed mechanism to be excluded from comparisons.
choices.rationale: Competing explanations and confounders still require attention; selection does not justify excluding them.

choices.text: A mechanism turns temporal association into explanation, with controlled comparisons mainly estimating the intervention's practical production cost.
choices.rationale: Comparisons test causality and competing explanations; mechanism proposals are not established facts.

choices.text: A load-heat mechanism identifies relevant measurements and comparisons, including observations that could challenge its expected link to failure.
choices.rationale: A hypothesis makes a testable prediction rather than merely listing patterns.

choices.text: A hypothesis reduces the dataset, making its remaining measurements independent enough to separate heat from machine-load changes.
choices.rationale: Smaller data are not automatically independent; credible measurements and comparisons are required.

questions.stem: Why should analysts deliberately look for observations that conflict with a preferred explanation?

choices.text: Contrary observations help add conditions after each result, preserving a mechanism's usefulness across increasingly diverse operating environments.
choices.rationale: Unrestricted post-hoc exceptions can make the hypothesis untestable.

choices.text: Contrary cases expose omitted conditions when exceptions produce measurable boundaries, rather than repeatedly shielding the explanation from possible challenge.
choices.rationale: A hypothesis becomes more informative when its limits are examined.

choices.text: Contrary cases reveal measurement errors, allowing researchers to retain the preferred mechanism once those cases have been excluded.
choices.rationale: They may reveal omitted conditions or challenge the mechanism; they cannot simply be excluded as errors.

choices.text: Conflicting cases establish whether chance correlations occurred, making a separate confirmation dataset unnecessary after enough examples are inspected.
choices.rationale: Counterexamples strengthen tests but do not replace independent confirmation or guarantee absence of chance patterns.

questions.stem: Why might a sensor reading fail to detect a real causal factor?

choices.text: A slow sensor may miss brief spikes, making added sensor numbers sufficient to resolve uncertainty about the proposed mechanism.
choices.rationale: Volume alone does not repair unsuitable placement, sampling or causal design.

choices.text: Casing temperature reflects internal heat imperfectly, so failures without detected heat provide decisive counterexamples to the mechanism.
choices.rationale: The instrument may miss causal heat; detecting capacity must be checked before interpreting absence.

choices.text: Sensor gaps may obscure timing, but operator reports can establish the missed physical change without checking their definitions.
choices.rationale: Reports have their own interpretation limits; sources may use different timing and terminology.

choices.text: Its placement or sampling rate may miss the relevant physical change, and gaps may occur under particular conditions.
choices.rationale: Measurement design can hide the signal or make missingness informative.

questions.stem: Which conclusion best answers the opening question?

choices.text: A broad sensor network supports explanation once patterns are confirmed, even if the measured variables poorly represent the proposed mechanism.
choices.rationale: Confirmation does not repair poor measurements; mechanism-relevant data are essential.

choices.text: Data can expand observation without explanation; knowledge advances when readings are tied to testable questions and comparisons.
choices.rationale: The answer distinguishes information quantity from explanatory design.

choices.text: Data become knowledge when several sources describe the same sequence, making interventions useful mainly for choosing practical responses.
choices.rationale: Agreement on sequence does not establish cause; interventions can distinguish explanations.

choices.text: Explanation advances when a smaller dataset captures the strongest association, reducing the chance patterns created by extensive observation.
choices.rationale: Smaller size or strongest association alone is insufficient; testable questions and credible comparisons matter.

passage.title: The Road That Followed an Ancient Tax Border

paragraphs.text: A modern road north of Padua bends at regular intervals across an otherwise open plain. Drivers may assume the turns follow a stream or a natural ridge, but maps show no obvious obstacle at each corner. Archaeologists studying Roman landscapes have found that some present-day roads preserve parts of ancient land divisions. The question is not simply whether an old line survives, but what kind of line it was and why later communities kept it.

Roman surveyors sometimes organized land into repeated blocks separated by boundary lines. These divisions could mark plots assigned to settlers, define rights of access, and support administration of land. In some settings, the recorded status of a parcel mattered for taxation or other obligations. The word “tax border” can therefore suggest more than a wall between two territories: it may refer to a surveyed line that helped identify land and its responsibilities.

When a new settlement was laid out, surveyors could establish major axes and divide nearby land in a regular pattern. Some alignments were carried by roads, paths, drainage channels, or field edges. A road following one of these lines did not necessarily begin as a road in the form seen today. It may have started as a boundary or track, been widened later, and then become part of a regional route.

This history creates a tempting explanation for the modern curve: perhaps the road bends because it follows an ancient cadastral line. But a similar shape can arise for other reasons. A route may skirt wet ground, connect older villages, avoid a property, or follow a later canal. A repeating grid is evidence of planning, not proof that every line belongs to one Roman survey or that a particular road served tax collection.

Researchers compare several kinds of evidence. Archaeological traces can include straight ditches, field edges, roads, boundary stones, or alignments visible in aerial images. Historical cadastral maps show later property divisions, while modern maps reveal which lines remain in use. Ancient texts describe surveying practices, but they do not identify every surviving feature on the ground. A convincing interpretation needs agreement among sources that were made at different times and for different purposes.

Terrain provides a competing explanation. A road may curve around a watercourse or use a dry route across a floodplain. If the same bend appears in a line of field boundaries that continues across small changes in elevation, a planned division becomes more plausible. If the bend tracks a slope or drainage channel, topography may better explain it. The comparison must use detailed elevation and hydrology data rather than treating a flat-looking map as proof that the land offered no obstacle.

Cadastral maps require their own scrutiny. Many were drawn centuries after Roman land division, and their purpose was often to record ownership, land use, or tax obligations in the period when the map was made. A boundary on a nineteenth-century map is not automatically ancient simply because it is straight. It can preserve an older line, but it can also reflect a later legal decision or modern surveying practice.

Map alignment also involves measurement error. Old sheets may have been copied, distorted, or drawn at different scales. Researchers georeference them by matching features that can still be identified, such as churches, rivers, or road junctions. If a map is stretched to fit too few landmarks, its apparent agreement with an ancient grid may be misleading. Analysts therefore test several control points and report how far the lines could shift.

The Roman grid itself is not always a perfect square imposed without regard to the landscape. Surveyors adapted plans to existing settlements, water access, property claims, and local conditions. A line that appears regular in one district may change direction in another. Researchers have to distinguish a broad design principle from a rigid template. Otherwise, they may force ambiguous roads into the pattern they expect to find.

The relationship between land division and taxation is also more complicated than a single border. Tax systems could distinguish parcels by status, yield, ownership, or exemption, and their rules changed over time. A surviving boundary might have helped officials or communities identify a parcel without marking a tax jurisdiction. The line’s function cannot be read directly from its shape; it must be inferred from documents, inscriptions, settlement patterns, and the arrangement of neighboring plots.

One way to compare explanations is to ask what each predicts beyond the road itself. A terrain account predicts a relation to slopes, streams, or ground conditions. A cadastral account predicts parallel or perpendicular lines repeated across fields, sometimes continuing beyond the modern road. A settlement account predicts connections among places that existed at the relevant time. If only one short curve matches a proposed grid, the evidence is weak; if a network of boundaries shares the alignment, the case improves.

Even a strong geometric fit does not establish uninterrupted use. A boundary could disappear and later be revived because it remained a convenient property edge. A medieval path might follow an older ditch without anyone remembering its Roman origin. Continuity of location is different from continuity of purpose. Archaeologists may identify an ancient alignment with confidence while remaining uncertain about exactly when it became a road or which administrative task it once served.

For modern planners, this distinction matters. If a route preserves an old boundary, widening it may erase evidence beyond the visible pavement, including ditches or field edges that explain the pattern. Yet not every curved lane needs to be protected as an ancient monument. Mapping the wider network and checking it on the ground can help separate a meaningful landscape feature from a coincidental resemblance.

The road’s shape can therefore be read as a possible trace of institutional history, but only through comparison. Cadastral maps may reveal property patterns; terrain data can test natural explanations; archaeological and written evidence can clarify dates and functions. The most defensible conclusion is conditional: an old land-division line may have guided a later route where multiple alignments coincide, but the surviving curve alone cannot prove a tax border or a continuous Roman road.

questions.stem: Why does the passage treat “tax border” as a broader idea than a boundary between territories?

choices.text: A surveyed line separated exempt land from taxable land, making its tax purpose recognizable from neighboring plot shapes.
choices.rationale: Possible statuses require documentary evidence; shapes alone cannot establish the specific purpose.

choices.text: A parcel line identified different tax jurisdictions even where later roads obscured the original territorial separation.
choices.rationale: Parcel obligations need not mark tax jurisdictions or territorial separation.

choices.text: Surveyed roads recorded the taxes collected from settlers, preserving administrative obligations whenever the road alignment survived.
choices.rationale: Location does not establish continued function, and the line need not originate as a road.

choices.text: Parcel lines could identify land status and obligations through boundaries or tracks without necessarily separating territories or tax jurisdictions.
choices.rationale: The passage links land status and administration while distinguishing territorial borders.

questions.stem: What would make a cadastral explanation more convincing than a terrain explanation?

choices.text: Repeated field alignments crossing elevation changes favor planned division over bends following drainage channels or other terrain constraints.
choices.rationale: That pattern better fits a planned division than a landform constraint.

choices.text: A single bend closely matches a Roman template after an old map is aligned to two surviving landmarks.
choices.rationale: A single match and too few control points can create misleading agreement.

choices.text: Several aligned boundaries track the same drainage channel, showing surveyors adapted the ancient grid to local terrain.
choices.rationale: This remains compatible with a terrain explanation and does not establish ancient planning.

choices.text: The road follows a straight ditch on a later cadastral map, even when nearby field boundaries differ.
choices.rationale: A later ditch may reflect drainage or later decisions; a broader repeated alignment is stronger.

questions.stem: Why must researchers treat later cadastral maps cautiously?

choices.text: Their boundaries usually preserve ancient locations, but copied scales can obscure whether those locations had continuous tax functions.
choices.rationale: Ancient location is itself uncertain; later creation and map distortion both need scrutiny.

choices.text: They record later ownership or tax conditions and may preserve, alter, or create boundaries after Roman times.
choices.rationale: The map’s date and purpose do not automatically establish an ancient origin.

choices.text: Their administrative purpose makes tax origins likely, although georeferencing must establish exactly where the Roman boundary ran.
choices.rationale: Later tax purposes do not establish Roman origin; georeferencing cannot supply an ancient date.

choices.text: They preserve later ownership accurately, so uncertainty concerns chiefly whether Roman surveyors used square or locally adapted grids.
choices.rationale: Later lines may be new or altered, and map distortion also matters.

questions.stem: What distinction does the passage make between spatial and functional continuity?

choices.text: A remembered Roman origin establishes functional continuity even if later communities move the road away from the surveyed boundary.
choices.rationale: Remembered origin is not the passage's criterion; function and location require separate evidence.

choices.text: A revived property edge preserves continuous spatial use, although its earlier tax obligations may have changed over time.
choices.rationale: A boundary may disappear and later revive; shared location does not establish uninterrupted use.

choices.text: A road can change width while retaining administrative continuity, provided the boundary remains visible on later property maps.
choices.rationale: Visible location or width does not prove continuity of purpose.

choices.text: A route may remain in the same place even if its original administrative purpose has been forgotten or replaced.
choices.rationale: Location can persist without continuous function or memory.

questions.stem: Which conclusion best explains how to interpret the road’s curve?

choices.text: Matching a wider field network establishes Roman origin, while written evidence is needed mainly to identify the taxes collected.
choices.rationale: A network strengthens the case but does not alone establish date or Roman origin.

choices.text: Terrain and cadastral evidence can establish the original purpose when both explain the same repeating bends around local obstacles.
choices.rationale: Spatial fit cannot directly establish original function; documents and archaeology are also needed.

choices.text: It may preserve a land-division alignment if independent spatial and historical evidence converges, but the curve alone is not proof.
choices.rationale: The conclusion is conditional and depends on multiple sources.

choices.text: Later changes may conceal the rest of the survey, so a defensible ancient alignment warrants preserving every nearby curve.
choices.rationale: The passage calls for distinguishing meaningful features from coincidental resemblance, not blanket protection.

passage.title: The Unexpected Winners of a Subsidy

paragraphs.text: The fictional city of Asterford expanded a rent subsidy to help low-income households remain near work and school. Eligible tenants could receive a monthly payment toward rent, while landlords continued to collect the full listed amount. The city expected the assistance to reach renters directly. Within a year, however, average rents had also risen in several eligible neighborhoods. Some residents argued that property owners had captured part of the benefit; city officials asked whether the subsidy itself had caused the increase.

A subsidy changes what some tenants can afford, but the effect on rent depends on the number of homes available and how quickly that number can change. If apartments are plentiful, a landlord may have to compete for tenants and accept a lower rent than requested. If housing is scarce, more households bidding for the same units may permit owners to raise prices. The payment’s value can therefore be shared between renters and landlords rather than reaching one group in full.

Asterford had added households to the program more quickly than it had approved new housing. Several years of restrictive zoning and slow permit review had limited construction in the central districts. Developers could build apartments in outer areas, but jobs and transit were concentrated downtown. The city had increased purchasing power in neighborhoods where demand was already high, while the supply of nearby homes could not expand quickly.

Still, the rent increase was not proof that landlords had raised prices because of the subsidy. Utility costs had risen, two large buildings were under renovation, and new employers had attracted additional residents. A rise could have occurred even without the policy. To estimate the subsidy’s effect, analysts needed a comparison that accounted for these other changes rather than comparing this year’s rent with last year’s alone.

The city compared eligible neighborhoods with similar areas where fewer households qualified. It tracked rent changes before and after the expansion, as well as vacancies, unit size, and distance from transit. The comparison suggested larger increases where vacancy rates were already low. But it was not a randomized experiment: neighborhoods differed in employment growth and building age, and some tenants moved across district lines. The result was evidence about a pattern, not a precise measure of how much each owner captured.

Tenant advocates emphasized that even a partially absorbed subsidy left some renters with more money for food, transport, or savings. A household could benefit although its landlord received a higher rent than before. Housing economists, by contrast, warned that the policy might become more expensive without making more units available. These claims were not contradictory. One concerned the immediate position of participating households; the other concerned how the benefit and cost might change as demand and prices adjusted.

The city considered capping the rent charged to households receiving assistance. A cap could prevent a landlord from raising the listed rent above a stated limit for those tenants. Yet owners might decline to rent to eligible households, convert units to another use, or maintain fewer apartments. A cap applied only to the program could also create two prices for similar homes. The city needed to consider how owners would respond, not only what the rule said.

A second proposal expanded eligibility to more households. If the increase in demand were spread across a wider market, advocates argued, landlords would have less reason to target the small group receiving aid. But broader eligibility would require more public money, and in a city with a fixed housing stock it could increase competition for available units. The outcome depended on whether additional supply arrived alongside the new payments.

A third proposal paired assistance with faster approvals for apartments near transit. The change would not add homes immediately: planning, financing, and construction take time. It could nevertheless make future supply more responsive if projects were completed. Residents raised concerns about displacement and infrastructure capacity. The city revised the proposal to include affordable units in new developments and to phase construction near schools and rail lines.

The city also examined who received the payments and who experienced the rent changes. Some eligible tenants lived in buildings whose rents rose little; others faced increases when leases renewed. Owners with vacant units could offer concessions, while owners in high-demand blocks had greater leverage. A citywide average blurred these differences. Officials began publishing rent and vacancy patterns by neighborhood and unit type, with safeguards to avoid identifying individual households.

After two years, the subsidy reduced the rent burden for many participating households, but the size of that reduction varied. Rents rose faster in some low-vacancy areas than in comparable neighborhoods; elsewhere, prices changed little. The city could not attribute every increase to the program. Its evaluation did suggest that the same payment produced different results depending on local supply conditions and landlord competition.

Budget officials proposed lowering the payment in neighborhoods where rents were rising fastest. Tenant groups warned that this would withdraw support precisely where housing was most expensive. A targeted adjustment could limit public spending, but might push families farther from transit and employment. The council instead kept the subsidy stable while changing eligibility rules for newly built units and dedicating funds to housing near transit.

No single change resolved the tension. Assistance could protect households in the short term, while new construction and transit investment addressed constraints over a longer period. Rent caps might protect some tenants but alter owners’ decisions. More payments could broaden access but also raise demand. Evaluators tracked both household budgets and housing supply, because success in one measure did not guarantee improvement in the other.

Asterford’s experience shows why the nominal recipient of a subsidy is not always its only beneficiary. When housing is scarce and supply responds slowly, owners may capture part of the payment through higher rents. But that does not mean tenants gain nothing or that every rent increase results from the subsidy. The distribution depends on vacancies, construction, location, and policy design. A durable evaluation must examine who benefits, which areas change, and whether the stock of homes can respond.

questions.stem: Why might a rent subsidy lead to higher rents in some Asterford neighborhoods?

choices.text: Expanded eligibility made renters less sensitive to location, allowing higher prices even in neighborhoods with many vacant apartments.
choices.rationale: Scarcity and low vacancies favored price increases; reduced location sensitivity is not established.

choices.text: Subsidies reduced tenants' rent burdens, encouraging landlords to raise prices chiefly to recover increased utility and renovation costs.
choices.rationale: Those costs were rival explanations; the subsidy mechanism concerned purchasing power against constrained supply.

choices.text: Payments increased purchasing power where restricted construction limited available homes, giving landlords greater leverage to raise rents amid scarcity.
choices.rationale: High demand and slow supply response can allow prices to rise.

choices.text: Payments increased demand near work, while faster outer-area construction made central landlords compete more strongly for eligible tenants.
choices.rationale: Outer construction did not rapidly expand scarce downtown supply; central leverage remained strong.

questions.stem: Why did analysts avoid treating the rent increase as proof of the subsidy’s effect?

choices.text: Neighborhood differences explained the entire rise, making pre-expansion rent trends more informative than changes following the subsidy.
choices.rationale: Other changes complicated causal inference but were not proven to explain the entire rise.

choices.text: Attribution of rent rises to subsidies was limited by changing costs and employment, neighborhood differences and tenant movements.
choices.rationale: The evaluation was suggestive but not a randomized test.

choices.text: Similar comparison areas established the subsidy's average effect, although individual leases prevented precise estimates for each household.
choices.rationale: The nonrandomized comparison was suggestive and still confounded, not an established average causal effect.

choices.text: The comparison showed stronger rises in low-vacancy areas, so uncertainty remained mainly about which owners raised their rents.
choices.rationale: Employment, building age, moving tenants and other causes limited attribution, not just owner identification.

questions.stem: How could tenants benefit even if landlords captured part of the subsidy?

choices.text: Higher rents increased landlord receipts but left tenants' total housing costs unchanged wherever the subsidy was fully absorbed.
choices.rationale: The question concerns partial capture; tenants could retain some relief, differing by market.

choices.text: Participating tenants gained through more available homes, although owners received most of the immediate monthly payment.
choices.rationale: The stock did not expand quickly; immediate tenant gains came from remaining rent relief.

choices.text: Subsidies improved household budgets because landlords in eligible areas competed for recipients despite low vacancy rates.
choices.rationale: Low vacancies gave owners leverage; relief could persist despite, not necessarily through, stronger competition.

choices.text: The payment could still reduce household rent burdens, although the amount of relief differed by market conditions.
choices.rationale: Partial capture does not imply zero benefit to tenants.

questions.stem: Why did the city pair rent assistance with faster approvals for housing near transit?

choices.text: Near-transit housing would lower program spending immediately, allowing assistance payments to be reduced in the highest-rent neighborhoods.
choices.rationale: Housing was a longer-term response, and the city kept subsidies stable.

choices.text: Additional approvals would limit landlord price increases directly, applying the same rent ceiling to new and existing assisted homes.
choices.rationale: Approvals addressed supply; program rent caps were a separate proposal with trade-offs.

choices.text: Faster approvals would spread subsidy demand across a wider market, avoiding the need to consider construction delays or displacement.
choices.rationale: Construction took time, and displacement and infrastructure concerns required revisions.

choices.text: Current rent relief from assistance could be complemented over time by completed near-transit housing loosening the supply constraints that shaped payment distribution.
choices.rationale: The policies targeted different time horizons and constraints.

questions.stem: Which conclusion best captures the passage’s account of subsidy outcomes?

choices.text: Who gains depends partly on local supply and competition, so evaluation should track tenants and housing conditions together.
choices.rationale: The conclusion connects distribution with market response.

choices.text: Tenant budget improvements establish success even when housing remains scarce, because supply measures concern a separate construction policy.
choices.rationale: Evaluators tracked both budgets and supply; success on one did not imply improvement on the other.

choices.text: Broader eligibility distributes benefits more fairly, with landlord capture becoming less important when assistance reaches a larger market.
choices.rationale: In fixed supply, broader payments can raise competition; capture remains dependent on conditions.

choices.text: Partial capture reduces assistance efficiency, so payments should decline fastest where low vacancies give property owners greater leverage.
choices.rationale: The city rejected this adjustment because it could withdraw support where costs were highest.

items.source: Evershed et al. (1992), Effects of migration of soil lipids on organic residues associated with buried potsherds; pottery lipid-residue methods and contamination controls in Archaeological and Anthropological Sciences (2021).

passage.title: What Residue on a Jar Cannot Prove

paragraphs.text: A pottery fragment may look empty, yet its porous walls can retain traces of substances once placed inside it. Archaeologists extract these residues and analyze molecules such as lipids, which occur in animal fats, plant oils, and other organic materials. A chemical signature can reveal clues about a vessel’s past use, but it is not a label attached by its ancient owner. The challenge is to determine what the residue indicates—and what it cannot establish by itself.

A jar that contains a pattern associated with animal fat may have held meat, milk products, or a mixture of ingredients. Different animals can produce similar broad chemical classes, while heating and burial alter molecules. More detailed measurements, including stable carbon isotope ratios, can help distinguish some sources. Still, a result usually identifies a range of plausible materials rather than a complete recipe. The same vessel could also have served different purposes during its lifetime.

Repeated cooking can leave an accumulated signal. A vessel used for fish one week and plants another might retain traces of both, with the stronger or more chemically persistent signal dominating analysis. The residue may represent several uses rather than the last meal prepared. Scraping, washing, reheating, and storage can change what remains. A researcher must therefore avoid reading one chemical profile as a precise snapshot of a single event.

Burial creates another source of uncertainty. Soil contains organic material from plants, microorganisms, and later activity. Some of these compounds can enter the porous ceramic after the vessel is discarded. If a sample from a pot resembles nearby soil, contamination becomes a concern; if the two differ, that supports—but does not automatically prove—a use-related origin. Sampling location matters, because the outside and inside surfaces may have different histories.

Laboratories reduce contamination in several ways. Researchers may clean the surface, remove the outer layer of a sherd, drill into the ceramic fabric, and run blank samples through the same preparation process. A blank contains no archaeological pottery but passes through laboratory equipment, revealing residues introduced during handling. Soil from the excavation can be analyzed as a comparison. These steps do not make contamination impossible; they let researchers identify some sources and judge the remaining risk.

The chemical instrument also has limits. It detects compounds that survive, can be extracted, and exceed its detection threshold. A substance that leaves little residue may be absent from the results even if it was once present. Different foods preserve differently, and the pottery’s clay and firing conditions affect absorption. “Not detected” therefore does not mean “never used.” It may mean that the relevant evidence did not survive or could not be measured with the chosen method.

To infer vessel function, archaeologists compare chemistry with shape and wear. A deep pot with heating damage may be consistent with cooking, while a narrow-necked jar could have supported storage or transport. Neither form determines use by itself: people can repurpose containers, and similar shapes can serve different tasks. Residues can refine the interpretation, while marks, residue locations, and breakage patterns provide additional clues.

Context is equally important. A jar found in a household room may have been used differently from a similar vessel in a burial or workshop. Animal bones, plant remains, hearths, and storage areas can establish what activities occurred nearby. If a lipid signal suggests aquatic resources but fish bones are scarce, that is not necessarily a contradiction: fish remains may preserve poorly or have been processed elsewhere. It is a reason to examine how each form of evidence was created and preserved.

A study of an archaeological jar can compare samples from several locations on the same vessel and from the surrounding soil. If the inner wall contains a distinctive signal absent from the soil and outer surface, the case for contents used inside becomes stronger. If every sample shares a broad profile, post-depositional contamination or a widespread environmental source becomes more plausible. Multiple samples do not tell the entire story, but they can reveal whether one small piece represents the whole object.

Control samples help define the background, but they must be chosen carefully. Soil collected far from a vessel may not represent the sediment that touched it. A modern laboratory blank can reveal contamination from equipment but not every chemical change that took place underground. Analysts need to record where samples came from and how they were handled. The comparison is only as informative as the match between the archaeological sample and its control.

Chemical detection also differs from cultural interpretation. Finding a marker associated with milk does not show who consumed it, whether it was ordinary or ceremonial, or how a community valued it. Those claims require evidence about household organization, trade, animal management, and the vessel’s archaeological context. A molecular result can make some interpretations more likely and rule out others, but it cannot supply social meaning without additional lines of evidence.

Researchers should report alternative explanations rather than only the favored one. A fatty residue could reflect cooking, storage, repair material, or later contamination, depending on its composition and location. These possibilities are not equally likely in every case. The point is to state what observations would distinguish them—for example, heating markers, interior distribution, comparison with soil, or residues in other vessels from the same context.

The strongest interpretation often comes from convergence. Molecular evidence may indicate a food group; animal bones identify available species; plant remains show what was processed; vessel shape suggests heating or storage. When independent clues agree, a specific account becomes more defensible. When they disagree, the mismatch may reveal mixed use, preservation bias, or an overly narrow interpretation.

A residue can show that certain compounds survived in a pot and, with careful controls, support an inference about past contents. It cannot alone reconstruct a meal or explain its cultural significance. Soil comparisons, blanks, sampling across the vessel, and archaeological context help separate use-related traces from contamination. The chemical signal is valuable precisely when its limits are respected: it adds one kind of evidence to a larger reconstruction, rather than replacing that reconstruction.

passage.title: The Game That Rewarded the Wrong Strategy

paragraphs.text: The fictional city of Norwick launched an energy-saving app that awarded points to apartment buildings whose residents reduced electricity use. A public board ranked buildings, and the highest scorers received funds for shared improvements. In the first month, reported consumption fell sharply in several buildings. But the pattern raised a puzzle: did residents change habits, or had some users learned how to improve their score without reducing the amount of energy the buildings actually used?

The app compared each building’s current meter reading with a baseline calculated from the previous year. One explanation was that competition made energy use visible. Residents reminded one another to turn off common-area lights and delayed running laundry machines until off-peak hours. If this explanation was right, the buildings with larger point gains should continue using less electricity after the competition ended, even when the app no longer awarded prizes.

A second explanation focused on the scoring rule. The baseline adjusted for temperature and occupancy, but residents could change how those factors were reported. A few building managers entered estimated occupancy late, after seeing the month’s energy use. Others temporarily moved activities to meters not included in the competition. If point gains depended on such changes, official scores could improve without a comparable reduction in total consumption.

The two explanations made different predictions. Genuine conservation should appear in whole-building meter records, including common spaces, and should not vanish when a bonus was removed. Score manipulation should be more visible in accounts that relied on self-reported values or excluded certain meters. Norwick’s first dashboard displayed points and submitted readings, but did not show whether the savings persisted or whether all electricity use had been counted.

The utility compared app scores with monthly meter data and found that some high-ranking buildings had reduced measured consumption. In several others, the app’s reported saving was larger than the decline at the main meter. Investigators traced part of the gap to an incorrectly updated occupancy baseline and part to laundry rooms supplied by separate meters. These findings did not show that every resident had cheated. They showed that the score could reward both real changes and the way a building was recorded.

When the city corrected the baseline, two buildings lost points and complained that the rules had changed after the contest. Their managers argued that they had followed the app’s instructions. Residents in those buildings had also reduced hallway lighting and adjusted heating schedules. A scoring correction could remove an unfair advantage while still failing to recognize genuine effort. Norwick had to separate the integrity of the measure from the question of whether useful behavior had occurred.

The city then ran a second round with a revised rule. Buildings had to connect all shared meters before entering the contest, and occupancy data came from a common administrative source. Scores were calculated only after a month had ended, preventing managers from changing inputs in response to the preliminary result. These changes made manipulation harder, but increased setup work and excluded several older buildings whose wiring could not be mapped quickly.

Some organizers proposed replacing the ranking with a cooperative target. Each building would receive funds if the city as a whole reduced use, regardless of whether it placed first. The proposal might discourage residents from competing over a tiny score difference and encourage them to share practical tips. But a collective reward could also let a high-consuming building benefit from reductions elsewhere. The city would need a rule for distributing funds and a way to keep each building accountable.

Norwick tested a hybrid: every building received a modest reward for meeting an adjusted reduction target, while a smaller bonus recognized unusually large verified savings. The baseline was fixed before the season, all meters were included, and an independent sample of readings was checked. The city also published uncertainty ranges because weather and occupancy estimates were not exact. A building near the threshold could not be classified with the same confidence as one far above it.

The hybrid changed the social atmosphere. Building representatives began exchanging information about insulation, boiler timing, and common-room lighting. Some residents reported that cooperation made conservation feel less like a contest among neighbors. Yet the app recorded energy, not the reasons for changes. The city could not tell from meter data alone whether residents had formed lasting habits, followed a building manager’s schedule, or simply shifted energy use to an uncounted place.

To test persistence, researchers compared use after rewards were reduced. Verified consumption remained lower in some buildings but returned toward baseline in others. Weather differed between periods, and several buildings made repairs during the same months. The comparison therefore suggested that at least part of the reduction lasted, but did not isolate the effect of points from maintenance, seasonal differences, or continued peer reminders.

The cooperative target also had an unintended distributional effect. Buildings with newer appliances could reach reductions more easily than buildings whose residents had little control over old heating systems. A uniform threshold could appear neutral while rewarding conditions that owners, not tenants, had chosen. Norwick added a small building-upgrade fund and reported results by building age, separating what residents controlled from the constraints they inherited.

The city did not abandon points, but changed what they represented. It treated a score as a prompt for action rather than proof of conservation. Public reports displayed verified meter changes, missing-meter warnings, and the duration of reductions. Residents could still earn recognition, but prizes depended on evidence that included shared spaces and did not rely solely on adjustable inputs. The design made the outcome less dramatic and the claim more defensible.

Norwick’s experiment revealed the paradox of incentives: a reward can motivate the behavior a city wants while encouraging people to optimize whatever the system measures. Competition may spur real savings, but a score built on incomplete or adjustable data can turn measurement into a strategy of its own. Cooperation can broaden participation yet obscure who contributed. Good design therefore combines meaningful rewards with verifiable outcomes, attention to unequal starting conditions, and follow-up after the prize disappears.

questions.stem: What would distinguish genuine conservation from score manipulation?

choices.rationale: Persistence and whole-meter changes are predictions of genuine conservation; corrected rankings alone are insufficient.

choices.rationale: Meter comparisons could not isolate cooperation, points, repairs, weather or reminders.

choices.text: Repairs, weather, and peer reminders changed too, so meter differences could not isolate the effect of points.

questions.stem: Which principle best captures Norwick’s revised use of incentives?

choices.text: Fixed inputs make scores reliable evidence of conservation, while building-age adjustments establish whether residents formed lasting habits.

choices.text: Cooperative targets align rewards with real savings, allowing persistence checks to replace independent meter verification in future rounds.

choices.text: Verified reductions justify recognition across buildings, with equal thresholds preserving fairness despite differences in residents' technical control.
choices.rationale: Equal thresholds can reward inherited equipment advantages; unequal control must be considered.

choices.text: Treat scores as prompts, verify outcomes independently, and account for unequal conditions and behavior after rewards end.

passage.title: The Puzzle of Falling Birth Rates in Prosperous Cities

paragraphs.text: Several prosperous cities have seen birth rates fall even as residents’ incomes and access to services remain high. The pattern challenges a simple expectation: if families have more money, they should find it easier to raise children. Income matters, but it is only one part of a decision that also involves housing, work, care, partnership, health, and personal preference. A city can be wealthy on average while many younger adults face conditions that make family formation difficult.

The first distinction is between national prosperity and the resources available to a household at the point when it considers having a child. A city’s average income can rise because high earners are concentrated in certain industries, while rents and home prices rise for everyone seeking space. Young adults may have stable employment but still lack savings for a deposit or a suitable apartment. Aggregate wealth says little about whether a particular household can predict its finances several years ahead.

Housing costs affect more than the monthly budget. A family may need an additional bedroom, access to childcare, or a short journey to work. In a dense city, the homes meeting those needs may be limited or expensive. Some couples delay moving in together or having a child until they can secure stable housing. This delay can reduce the number of years available for family plans, even when people still want children.

Employment adds another layer. A secure job can provide income and benefits, but long or unpredictable hours make it difficult to arrange care. Temporary contracts can make future plans uncertain even when current pay is adequate. When one parent is expected to remain available late, the other may absorb more childcare and face a career penalty. The effect depends not only on whether people work, but on schedule control, leave access, and how care is divided.

Housing and work pressures reinforce one another. An affordable home may be far from employment, extending commutes and narrowing time for care. A central home may shorten travel but consume more income. If childcare closes before a shift ends, a household needs backup care or relatives. A wage increase alone may not resolve this coordination problem.

Norms and preferences also shape decisions. In some workplaces, taking leave can be viewed as a lack of commitment; in some households, expectations about who provides care remain unequal even when both adults work. People may adapt their plans to these expectations or decide that the costs are too high. Researchers cannot infer a private preference directly from a birth rate. The same outcome may reflect a choice, a postponed intention, or a constraint that prevented a desired family plan.

This helps explain why higher income does not guarantee more births. Additional income may make childcare and housing more affordable, but it can also arrive alongside longer work hours or higher living costs. A household may value education, leisure, or career stability and decide to have fewer children. Another may want more children but postpone the decision until housing or work becomes more predictable. The relationship between income and fertility can therefore differ across groups and stages of life.

Cross-country analyses find that labor conditions and family policies move alongside fertility trends, but association does not prove causation. Countries differ in housing markets, partnership age, norms, and economic shocks. Policies may also respond to declining births. Comparisons can identify patterns worth investigating, but cannot predict what will happen if a city copies one policy.

Timing creates a further complication. The total fertility rate for a year can fall when people postpone births, even if some later have the children they intended. A measure of births in one period is not identical to the completed family size of a generation. If the average age at childbirth rises, yearly rates may temporarily reflect delay as well as a lasting change in how many children people have. Analysts need to distinguish these possibilities before describing a trend.

A city can compare reported intentions with conditions residents face. Surveys may ask what prevents a desired family plan, while administrative data show rents, childcare, leave use, and job security. Intentions may change, and records may miss informal care or private household negotiations. Combining sources is more informative than treating one indicator as a motive.

Policy options work through different mechanisms. Housing support can reduce a family’s cost burden, while childcare services can lower both expense and scheduling difficulty. Paid leave may protect income during care, but its effect depends on who can use it and whether returning workers face penalties. More predictable schedules can help households coordinate, even without changing total wages. No single measure addresses all these channels, and a policy that helps one group may miss another.

Evaluation must also consider who benefits. A housing allowance can improve affordability for current tenants but may be partly absorbed into rents where supply is restricted. A childcare place helps only if its hours match work schedules and it is reachable. Leave that replaces little income may be formally available but practically unusable for low-paid workers. The design details determine whether a benefit changes the constraints that shaped a family’s decision.

Finally, a lower birth rate is not a diagnosis of social failure. People may freely choose smaller families, and policy should not treat their lives as instruments for a demographic target. The relevant public questions include whether people can have the family they want, whether care is shared fairly, and how institutions adapt to an older population. Those questions require evidence about both preferences and barriers, not only a count of births.

The puzzle in prosperous cities has no single solution because the decision is made where several conditions meet. Income can expand options, while high housing costs, insecure work, rigid schedules, and unequal care can narrow them. These forces interact: changing one may help only when another constraint also shifts. Birth-rate trends can reveal that conditions are changing, but they cannot identify the cause by themselves. A careful explanation separates preference, timing, and constraint before drawing conclusions.

questions.stem: How can housing costs affect family plans beyond reducing disposable income?

choices.rationale: Housing stability and other interacting barriers also matter; transport is not the sole cause.

choices.text: Stable employment offsets expensive housing, leaving childcare availability as the main remaining reason couples postpone having children.
choices.rationale: Housing, deposits, commute and predictability remain constraints despite stable employment.

choices.rationale: Housing shapes location, predictability, and coordination as well as cost.

choices.text: Higher prices encourage central living, reducing commuting time enough to compensate for delayed access to a larger family home.
choices.rationale: Central homes cost more; no general compensation for housing delay is established.

questions.stem: Why does the passage caution against reading a birth-rate outcome as a direct measure of preference?

choices.text: Postponement reflects chosen timing, whereas housing and care barriers affect family size only after a household has children.
choices.rationale: Constraints can delay desired family formation before children arrive.

choices.text: Reported intentions remain stable, while employment conditions determine whether those preferences appear in the next year's fertility measure.
choices.rationale: Intentions can change, and employment is one of several influences.

choices.text: Higher earners usually prefer smaller families, so aggregate birth rates reveal preferences once households' income differences are considered.
choices.rationale: Even within income groups constraints and timing differ; outcome is not a direct preference measure.

choices.text: The same outcome may reflect a chosen family size, delayed timing, or constraints that blocked an intended plan.
choices.rationale: Observed births do not reveal motivation by themselves.

questions.stem: What can cross-country fertility comparisons show, according to the passage?

choices.text: Comparisons can separate preference from delay using yearly rates, while local surveys mainly verify the inferred reasons for postponement.
choices.rationale: Yearly rates cannot independently separate delay, preference and constraints; surveys add imperfect evidence.

choices.text: Associations reveal patterns worth investigating, but contextual differences, policy responses and delayed births limit causal claims about policy effects.
choices.rationale: Associations guide inquiry without proving a policy effect.

choices.text: Comparisons identify household barriers reliably, but cities must adjust successful policies for local housing prices before copying them.
choices.rationale: Aggregate patterns do not reliably identify household barriers or establish policy success.

choices.text: Comparisons establish which policies raised yearly fertility, though completed family size is needed to estimate the size of that effect.
choices.rationale: Confounding and policy responses prevent simple causal establishment, apart from timing measures.

questions.stem: Why might a formally available family policy fail to ease a household’s constraint?

choices.text: Formal benefits leave barriers intact when childcare hours conflict with work or leave offers inadequate income and career protection.
choices.rationale: Access on paper does not ensure usability.

choices.text: Formal benefits fail mainly when their monetary value is low, since increased household income resolves service-location and schedule problems.
choices.rationale: Coordination and reachability can remain despite higher income.

choices.text: A reachable childcare place removes scheduling barriers, leaving leave eligibility as the chief determinant of practical policy access.
choices.rationale: Childcare hours must match work too; leave replacement and return penalties also matter.

choices.text: Paid leave protects earnings during care, so any remaining career penalties affect preference rather than the policy's practical usefulness.
choices.rationale: Return penalties can constrain practical use and family plans; they are not merely preferences.

questions.stem: Which conclusion best captures the passage’s explanation of falling birth rates in prosperous cities?

choices.text: Prosperity interacts with housing, work and care; birth trends still require distinguishing preferences, postponed plans and constraints blocking intentions.
choices.rationale: The conclusion rejects a single-cause account.

choices.text: Yearly declines reveal delayed family formation, while household surveys establish whether prosperity will eventually increase completed family size.
choices.rationale: Yearly declines can involve lasting change, and surveys do not establish future completed size.

choices.text: Prosperity makes smaller families more attractive, with expensive housing chiefly determining when those freely chosen plans are carried out.
choices.rationale: Some plans reflect blocked intentions, not only free preference or housing-based timing.

choices.text: Interacting barriers explain lower births, so successful policy should restore earlier rates by removing housing and work constraints together.
choices.rationale: Lower rates are not automatically failure; freely chosen smaller families and adapting institutions matter too.
